title: TypeScript skill test
summary: A timed practice assessment: multiple-choice questions on JavaScript runtime behaviour, the type system, generics, narrowing, variance, enums and tsconfig, plus two short coding tasks.

questions.explain: `var` is function-scoped, so all three closures share one `i`, which is 3 when they run. With `let`, each iteration gets a fresh binding and this prints `0 1 2`.

questions.prompt: A function reads a `let` variable on a line before that variable's declaration has run. What happens?
choices: It throws a `ReferenceError`: the binding is in its temporal dead zone
It reads an outer variable with the same name
questions.explain: `let`, `const` and `class` bindings are hoisted to the top of their block but stay uninitialised until the declaration runs. Any read before that throws a `ReferenceError`, and the inner binding still shadows an outer one with the same name.
Each call to `counter` creates a new `n`, and the returned functions close over that call's variable. `a` and `b` therefore keep separate counts.

questions.code:
console.log(greet())
function greet() { return 'hi' }
questions.explain: Function declarations are hoisted with their body, so they can be called before the line that declares them. A function expression assigned to `const` would throw, because the binding is still in its temporal dead zone.

questions.prompt: This compiles. What happens when the last line runs? (Class bodies are always strict mode.)
questions.explain: `this` is set by how a function is called, not where it is defined. A plain call `fn()` passes `undefined` in strict code, so `this.ticks` throws. Use `t.tick.bind(t)`, an arrow-function field, or call it as `t.tick()`.

An arrow function has no `this` of its own; it uses the `this` of the constructor that created it. That keeps it bound when detached, at the cost of one function per instance instead of one shared prototype method.
A bound function ignores any later `this` passed through `call`, `apply` or another `bind`. Only `new` can override a bound `this`.
The instance's prototype is `B.prototype`, whose prototype is `A.prototype`. `super.hi()` looks the method up on the parent prototype and calls it with the same `this`.

questions.code:
const n = Number('abc')
console.log(n === n, Object.is(n, n), [n].includes(n), [n].indexOf(n))
questions.explain: `NaN` is the only value not equal to itself under `===`, and `indexOf` uses `===`. `Object.is` and `includes` use SameValueZero-style rules that treat `NaN` as equal to itself. Use `Number.isNaN` to test for it.

questions.prompt: Which of these comparisons is `true` in JavaScript?
questions.explain: `null` and `undefined` are loosely equal to each other and to nothing else, which is why `x == null` is a common shorthand for "null or undefined". `null == 0` is `false` even though `null >= 0` is `true`.
`===`, `==` and `includes` all treat `0` and `-0` as equal. `Object.is(0, -0)` is `false`, and `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is `true`.

questions.code:
const parts = ['5', '2']
console.log(parts[0] + 1, Number(parts[1]) + 1, +parts[0] - +parts[1])
questions.explain: `+` with a string operand concatenates, and TypeScript allows `string + number`. Unary `+` and `Number()` convert explicitly. TypeScript would reject `parts[0] - 1`, because arithmetic needs number operands.

questions.code:
console.log('A')
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0)
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('C'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('D'))
console.log('E')
questions.explain: Synchronous code runs first (A, E). Then the microtask queue drains in order of queuing (C, D). Timers are tasks, so B runs after every microtask.

questions.code:
async function f() {
  console.log('1')
  await null
  console.log('2')
}
f()
console.log('3')
questions.explain: An async function runs synchronously until its first `await`. The rest of the body is queued as a microtask, even when the awaited value is not a promise.

questions.prompt: Code queues a `setTimeout(fn, 0)`, then starts a microtask that re-queues itself with `queueMicrotask` forever. What happens to `fn`?
choices: It runs after the next microtask
It never runs: the microtask queue never empties, so the loop never reaches the timer
It runs after about 4 ms regardless
questions.explain: The event loop drains the whole microtask queue before taking the next task. A microtask that keeps queuing microtasks starves timers, I/O and rendering. Recursive `setTimeout` yields between steps instead.
Microtasks queued while draining the queue (p2) run in the same drain, before any timer. `t1` was queued before `t2`, so it runs first.

questions.prompt: `Promise.all([a, b, c])` is awaited. `b` rejects while `a` and `c` are still pending. What happens?
choices: The returned promise rejects with `b`'s reason at once; `a` and `c` keep running
It waits for all three, then rejects with an array of results
questions.explain: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any input rejects. Promises cannot be cancelled, so the other work continues and its results are dropped. Use `Promise.allSettled` to wait for every outcome, or an `AbortSignal` to stop work.
`allSettled` never rejects. Each entry is `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`, and TypeScript narrows on `status`.

questions.prompt: This compiles. What is wrong with it?
choices: `forEach` awaits each callback, so the saves run one at a time
Nothing: `await` inside the callback makes `forEach` wait
`forEach` ignores the returned promises, so `done` logs before the saves finish and failures go unhandled
questions.explain: `forEach` calls the callback and discards its return value. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(ids.map(save))` for parallel work.

questions.prompt: `fetchText()` returns a promise that rejects. What does `load()` do?
choices: It resolves to a pending promise
It rejects with the same error: the `catch` never runs
questions.explain: Returning a promise without `await` leaves the `try` block before the promise settles, so its rejection skips the `catch`. Write `return await fetchText()` inside `try`/`catch`.

questions.code: console.log([10, 9, 1, 2].sort().join(' '))
questions.explain: Without a comparator, `sort` converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so `"10"` sorts before `"2"`. Pass `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers.
Maps and sets compare keys by identity (SameValueZero), not by structure. Two object literals are different keys; `1` and `'1'` are different values, and the repeated `1` is dropped.

questions.prompt: What does `new Array(3).map((_, i) => i)` return?
choices: An array of three empty slots: `map` skips holes
questions.explain: `new Array(3)` has length 3 but no elements, and `map`, `forEach` and `filter` skip missing indexes. `Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i)` builds `[0, 1, 2]`.

questions.prompt: Which array method returns a sorted copy and leaves the original unchanged?
questions.explain: `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` mutate in place. ES2023 added copying versions: `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with`.

choices: Any value can be assigned to it, but you must narrow it before using it as a specific type
Nothing can be assigned to it
It is only allowed in `catch` clauses
questions.explain: `unknown` is the safe top type: everything is assignable to it, but you cannot call it, index it or pass it on as a narrower type until a check such as `typeof` or a type guard narrows it. `any` switches checking off in both directions.

questions.code:
interface Point { x: number; y: number }
const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }
choices: No: a fresh object literal gets an excess property check, so `z` is an error
Yes: extra properties are fine structurally
No: `z` must be declared optional first
Yes, and `z` is removed at runtime
questions.explain: Structural typing allows extra properties in general, but an object literal assigned directly to a typed target is checked for unknown keys because they are usually typos. Assigning the same object through a variable compiles.

questions.code:
let a = 'x'
const b = 'x'
const c = { kind: 'x' }
type T = [typeof a, typeof b, typeof c.kind]
questions.explain: A `const` primitive keeps its literal type because it cannot change. `let` widens to `string`, and object properties widen too because they are mutable. `as const` on the object would keep `"x"`.

questions.code: type T = string & number
questions.explain: No value is both a string and a number, so the intersection is empty: `never`. It is also the type left after narrowing removes every member of a union, which is what exhaustiveness checks rely on.
The array literal `[1, 'a']` has type `(string | number)[]`, so `T` is `string | number` and the return type adds `undefined`.

choices: No: `T` is inferred from the first argument as `number[]`, so `'abc'` is rejected
questions.explain: When candidates for one type parameter share no common supertype, TypeScript does not invent a union; it picks one and reports the other argument. Use two type parameters, or pass `<number[] | string>` explicitly.
`K` is inferred as the literal `"name"`, so the indexed access `T[K]` picks that property's type. The object's properties widened to `number` and `string` when `T` was inferred.
A `const` type parameter infers as if the argument were written `as const`, so the array becomes a readonly tuple of literals. The `readonly` constraint lets that inferred type satisfy it.

choices: No: the function lacks an ending return statement
Yes: the switch covers every `kind`, so the end of the function is unreachable
questions.explain: Checking the discriminant narrows each case to one member, and TypeScript knows an exhaustive switch cannot fall through. Add a member to `Shape` and the function stops compiling, which is the point.

choices: No: `typeof null` is `'object'`, so `x` may still be `null`
Yes, and it returns 0 for arrays
questions.explain: TypeScript models the old JavaScript quirk: `typeof x === 'object'` keeps `null` in the union. Check `x !== null` or `Array.isArray(x)` instead.

questions.prompt: With TypeScript 5.5 or later, what is `R`?
questions.code:
const xs = [1, null, 2].filter(x => x !== null)
type R = typeof xs
questions.explain: Since 5.5, TypeScript infers a type predicate (`x is number`) from a simple arrow function like this one, and `filter` has an overload that uses it. Older versions needed an explicit `(x): x is number =>` guard.

questions.prompt: `Cat` and `Dog` are interfaces, and only `Dog` has a `bark` method. Which check narrows `pet: Cat | Dog` to `Dog`?
questions.explain: The `in` operator narrows to the union members that declare the property. Interfaces do not exist at runtime, so `instanceof Dog` and `constructor === Dog` are errors, and `typeof` only returns built-in tags.

questions.code:
type Opt<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }
type R = Opt<{ a: number; b: string }>['a']
questions.explain: The `?` modifier makes each property optional, and reading an optional property includes `undefined`. This is how the built-in `Partial<T>` is defined.

questions.code:
type ToArray<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never
type R = ToArray<string | number>
questions.explain: A conditional type over a naked type parameter distributes over a union, applying to each member separately. Wrap both sides, `[T] extends [unknown]`, to get `(string | number)[]` instead.

questions.code:
type Ret<F> = F extends (...args: never[]) => infer X ? X : never
type R = Ret<() => Promise<number>>
questions.explain: `infer X` captures the return type as written, which is the promise itself. Unwrapping it needs `Awaited<...>`, which is how `Awaited<ReturnType<F>>` is usually combined.

questions.code:
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] }
type R = keyof Getters<{ name: string; age: number }>
questions.explain: The `as` clause remaps each key through a template literal type. `string & K` keeps only string keys, because `Capitalize` cannot take numbers or symbols.

choices: No: under `strict`, `err` is `unknown` and must be narrowed first
No: a catch variable needs a type annotation
questions.explain: `strict` includes `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, because anything can be thrown. Narrow with `err instanceof Error` before reading `message`.

questions.prompt: Module `a` exports `let count = 0` and a function that increments it. Module `b` imports both, calls the function, then reads `count`. What does it see?
choices: `0`: imports are copies made at import time
`1`: ES module imports are live, read-only bindings
questions.explain: An ES module import is a live view of the exporter's variable, so updates made inside `a` are visible in `b`. `b` cannot assign to `count` itself. CommonJS `require` copies the value instead.
The `cause` option (ES2022) wraps a low-level error in a higher-level one without losing the original. `cause` is typed `unknown`, so it needs its own narrowing.

questions.prompt: With `verbatimModuleSyntax` on, why must `import { User } from './types'` become `import type { User }` when `User` is only an interface?
choices: Type imports make the checker faster
Without it, `User` would be checked as `any`
Interfaces can only be imported from `.d.ts` files
Imports are emitted as written, and at runtime `./types` has no `User` export
questions.explain: Under `verbatimModuleSyntax` the compiler never drops imports on its own. A value import of a type would remain in the JavaScript and fail or pull in a module for nothing, so type-only imports must say so.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a `private x` field and a `#x` field?
choices: `private` is checked only by the compiler; `#x` is enforced by the JavaScript runtime
questions.explain: `private` disappears when compiled, so the property is still reachable with a cast or from JavaScript. `#x` is a real private name: outside the class body it is a syntax error, and it also makes the class nominal for type compatibility.

choices: Nothing: parameter properties exist only in types
questions.explain: Parameter properties compile to assignments in the constructor, whatever their modifier. `private` only affects type checking, so `age` is an ordinary enumerable property at runtime.

questions.code:
abstract class Shape { abstract area(): number }
class Square extends Shape {}
choices: No: `Square` must implement `area` or be declared abstract
No: abstract classes cannot be extended
questions.explain: An abstract member has no implementation, so every concrete subclass has to provide one. The error appears at the class declaration rather than when `area` is called.

choices: Yes: classes are compared by structure, and both have the same shape
questions.explain: TypeScript compares class instance types structurally, like interfaces. A `private`, `protected` or `#private` member makes the comparison nominal, because such a member only matches its own declaration.

questions.code:
enum Color { Red, Green }
console.log(Object.keys(Color).length)
questions.explain: A numeric enum compiles to an object with both directions: `Red: 0`, `Green: 1`, `"0": "Red"` and `"1": "Green"`. String enum members get no reverse mapping.

questions.code:
enum Mode { On = 'ON', Off = 'OFF' }
const m: Mode = 'ON'
choices: No: string enum members are nominal, so a plain string is not assignable
questions.explain: String enums are deliberately opaque: you must write `Mode.On`. A union of string literals or an `as const` object accepts the plain string instead.

questions.code:
const Mode = { On: 'on', Off: 'off' } as const
type Mode = (typeof Mode)[keyof typeof Mode]
type R = Mode
questions.explain: `as const` keeps the literal values, and indexing by `keyof typeof Mode` collects them into a union. Declaring a type and a value with the same name gives an enum-like API with plain JavaScript output.

questions.prompt: Why is a `const enum` exported from a library risky for code built by a per-file transpiler (with `isolatedModules`)?
choices: Uses are inlined from the enum declaration, which a transpiler seeing one file at a time cannot read
Const enums cannot hold string values
Const enums always emit reverse mappings
questions.explain: A `const enum` has no runtime object; the compiler replaces each use with its value by reading the declaration. Single-file tools cannot do that across files, and inlined values go stale when the library changes.

choices: No: arrow functions cannot be assigned to a type alias
No: under `strictFunctionTypes`, function-type parameters are checked contravariantly
questions.explain: A `Handler` may be called with any `Animal`, and this function would call `bark` on a cat. A function is only safe to substitute when it accepts at least the parameter types of the target.

choices: No: it is the same as a function-typed property
No: the object literal has an excess property
Yes: parameters of method-syntax members stay bivariant even under `strictFunctionTypes`
questions.explain: `strictFunctionTypes` only applies to function types, not to methods declared with method syntax, so this unsound assignment compiles. Writing `handle: (a: Animal) => void` makes it an error.

choices: Yes: arrays are treated covariantly, so this unsound push type-checks
questions.explain: Mutable arrays should be invariant, but TypeScript treats them covariantly for convenience. `dogs` now holds a value without `bark`. Taking `readonly Animal[]` in APIs makes the covariance safe.

questions.prompt: What do the `in` and `out` modifiers do in `interface Box<in out T>`?
choices: They declare the type parameter's variance, which TypeScript checks and then uses instead of measuring it
questions.explain: `out` means covariant, `in` contravariant, and both together invariant. The compiler verifies the annotation against the type's structure, and it can speed up checking of deep recursive types.

questions.prompt: A project sets `"target": "ES2017"` and `"lib": ["ES2023"]`, then calls `items.findLast(...)`. What happens?
choices: It type-checks, but throws at runtime on engines without `findLast`: `lib` adds types, not polyfills
It fails to compile, because the target is too old
The call is removed from the output
questions.explain: `target` controls which syntax is downlevelled; `lib` only tells the checker which built-in APIs exist. Missing runtime APIs need a polyfill or a newer runtime.

questions.prompt: What does `declare module 'legacy-lib' { export function run(): void }` in a `.d.ts` file do?
choices: It creates a module named `legacy-lib` at runtime
It installs the package's published types
It describes the types of an untyped package, without emitting any code
questions.explain: An ambient module declaration tells the checker what an import of that name provides. Nothing is emitted, so it is only a promise about the real package, and a wrong declaration fails at runtime.
It skips checking every `.d.ts` file, which speeds builds and silences conflicts between dependencies' typings. Your `.ts` code is still checked against those declarations.

questions.prompt: With `strict` on but `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (it is not part of `strict`), what is `R`?
questions.code:
const arr: string[] = []
const x = arr[0]
type R = typeof x
questions.explain: By default, indexing an array or record is assumed to hit. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adds `| undefined` to such reads, which catches out-of-range bugs at the cost of more narrowing.
